title: MB5-03452
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who is a 25-year-old citizen of Peru and is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant is Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who is a 25-year-old citizen of Peru and is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant has presented new evidence and has requested an oral hearing.

With respect to the RPD's credibility assessment, which is the determinative issue in this claim, the RPD did not believe that the Appellant was at risk of persecution or at risk for an IRPA Section 97 reason because it concluded that the Appellant did not meet his burden of establishing that his story was true on a balance of probability. Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a Convention Refugee pursuant to s. 96 of IRPA, nor a person in need of protection pursuant to s. 97 of the IRPA.
The Appellant alleges that if he returns to Peru he will be targeted and perhaps killed by an individual, identified as Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX, and a street gang, identified as the XXXX de Puerto Nuevo.

The Appellant alleges that he was first targeted by Mr. XXXX in July of 2010 when he was visiting family in the Puerto Nuevo section of Lima. The Appellant alleges he was robbed at knifepoint and cut by Mr. XXXX. The Appellant alleges that he was assaulted twice more before January 2011 when he was assaulted for a fourth time but this time with a gun.

The Appellant alleged that at this point he made a police complaint but that, as a result, he and his business were the target of retaliation threats and extortion. The Appellant, fearing for his life, took the opportunity to work and study in Canada. The Appellant alleges that he hoped the situation would improve but when additional threats arrived along with the recognition that crime was out of control in Peru, the Appellant reached the conclusion that he was too much at risk in Peru, therefore he submitted a protection claim in Canada in XXXX 2015.

With respect to an outcome to this appeal, the Appellant argues that the RAD should "accept" the refugee claim of the Appellant. REQUEST TO SUBMIT NEW EVIDENCE NEW EVIDENCE AND REQUEST FOR AN ORAL HEARING

New evidence has being introduced in this appeal based on Section 110(4). This evidence includes three police reports. The first is the report (Appellant's Record, p. 16-19) that matches up with news articles (RPD Record, p. 103-109) related to the police arrest of Mr. XXXX and his two accomplices in January 2014. In addition, there is a case involving Mr. XXXX assaulting his wife (Appellant's Record, p. 20-23) in which Mr. XXXX was arrested. There is also a further arrest report, dated in August 2015, which is similar to the January 2014 arrest where Mr. XXXX is caught with an accomplice and there is evidence that Mr. XXXX was trafficking drugs.

I conclude that all of this material meets the legislative test of section 110(4) for admission given that the second and third police reports are new in that they date from after the RPD decision. The first case has a printing date after the RPD decision and although no explanation is offered, I would accept that this case would be best accessed as part of a police record check of Mr. XXXX that became useful followed the two arrests which come after the RPD decision. I find therefore that the first case meets the legislated test of section 110(4) because it was not reasonable available until Mr. XXXX was arrested on other charges.

Although I am accepting all this material, I conclude that this material is insufficient to require a hearing because this material cannot provide the bases to reverse the RPD's existing decision. The first case simply provides detail to what was already in the RPD record. The two new cases do not provide the bases to address the core credibility issue that the RPD has identified. This is that the story of the risk to the Appellant from Mr. XXXX is not credible. This can be seen in inconsistency, omission and the behaviour of the Appellant, which is not consistent with the behaviour of an individual facing risk. The new evidence is focused on the situation of Mr. XXXX and does not provide evidence establishing that Mr. XXXX had some dealings with the Appellant. I am therefore denying the request for an oral hearing under s. 110(6).

I note that the RAD has now received Federal Court guidance on the role of the RAD vis-à-vis RPD decisions. Justice Phelan in Huruglica1 states that the RAD "must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection". Justice Phelan suggests that while the RAD might show some deference on a credibility assessment and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion, in other areas, such as an assessment of country conditions evidence, the RAD need not be deferential.
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE AND FUNCTION OF THE RAD

paragraphs.text: In Njeukam,2 Justice Locke references Huruglica and suggests that "Except in cases where the credibility of a witness is critical or determinative or when the RPD has a particular benefit from the RAD to draw a specific conclusion, the RAD must not give any deference to the analysis of the evidence made by the RPD".

Following Huruglica and Njeukam, I conclude that where in this appeal the issue turns on questions of fact, specifically the RPD's assessment of the credibility of the Appellant when applied to the specific situation of the Appellant, the RPD's determinative credibility assessment must be granted deference, and I must provide my own assessment of the evidence. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL Core Issue: Did the Board err in its credibility conclusion?

In reading the RPD's decision the core reasoning is that it found too many consistency, omission and logic problems with the allegations when closely reviewed comparing the BOC narrative and testimony to conclude that this is a true story, on a balance of probability. From this perspective, the RPD reviewed the corroborative evidence and found that it was not sufficiently authoritative to set aside the identified credibility issues.

I note that the Appellant has not directly challenged the credibility concerns identified by the RPD. This includes inconsistencies between when the Appellant sets out in the narrative that he started to receive extortion demands and when the Appellant states in testimony these began (RPD Decision, paragraph 22). There is also the omission, which the RPD views as important, in the narrative of a reference to five 'written demands' from Mr. XXXX or his associates identified by the Appellant during testimony (RPD Decision, paragraph 25). The RPD also notes that the Appellant travelled on several occasions but did not seek to remain at his destination where perhaps he might have made an asylum claim. The RPD also identified a credibility problem in the fact that the Appellant returns multiple times to the area where he is allegedly in danger. For example, in January 2011 the Appellant travels to visit family members in Puerto Nuevo even though he alleges that he had been assaulted there on three previous visits (RPD Decision, paragraph 28).

In his Memorandum, the Appellant focuses on questioning the fact that the RPD did not find that the corroborative evidence was sufficient to set aside these identified credibility problems. The Appellant makes specific reference to Exhibit P-3 and argues that the RPD did not give "serious reasons" for why this Exhibit was given little weight (Appellant's Memorandum, paragraph 8).

With respect to exhibit P-3, which is a 'denunciation' to the police of the assault the Appellant allegedly faced in January 2011 (RPD Record, p. 96), the RPD identifies a credibility problem. The RPD notes that the reason the Appellant gives in testimony for not having made a police report after a prior robbery incident, which allegedly took place in July 2010, is that he was threatened and afraid. In the denunciation, however, it is written that the Appellant simply did not have the time to report it earlier.

Because the RPD finds a problem with this document coupled with the observation that a 'denunciation' "is not independent evidence of the occurrence of the events", the RPD does not accept this exhibit as probative (RPD Decision, paragraph 34).

The RPD then goes on to dismiss the "request for guarantees" which is allegedly a document required by the police to proceed with their investigation (RPD Record, p. 102), as lacking in probative value because it is not a certified true copy and it is signed only by the Appellant (RPD Decision, paragraph 34). I do not view the RPD's conclusions on these issues as errors because the RPD has identified real problems with these documents.

In addition, I would note an additional potential problem with Evidence P-3 in that while it mentions "XXXX XXXX" as the aggressor, there is no mention of Mr. XXXX or that this individual is somehow connected to the Puerto Nuevo gang. This bridge is accomplished in the corroborative evidence in the 'request for guarantees' document, which the RPD does not find probative because it does not have the same level of authentication as Exhibit P-3. Specifically, Exhibit P-3 is accepted as genuine but the contents are viewed as not necessarily true. The request for guarantees (Exhibit P-4) is found not sufficiently genuine to be accepted as probative.

The question which might be raised is that perhaps the Appellant did make a denunciation in 2011 but not against Mr. XXXX because these are two different people. While there is substantial evidence of the existence of Mr. XXXX XXXX this alias of 'XXXX XXXX' is not mentioned in the news articles or the arrest records for Mr. XXXX. After all, the Appellant is alleging that everyone around knew about XXXX XXXX (Oral hearing at minute 29-32), yet in the denunciation the Appellant has not identified XXXX XXXX as Mr. XXXX.

I would also note that XXXX XXXX in Exhibit 3 is described as acting alone and "lurks around at the same place every time he goes to visit his relative" (RPD Record, p. 96). In the corroborative evidence, however, Mr. XXXX has been arrested twice in his car with other gang members and he is clearly a seller of drugs, specifically 'PBC' (pasta base de cocaína - cocaine base paste - 'paco'). My point would be that there are alternate ways in which it might be possible to conclude that Exhibit P-3 is genuine but not probative to the allegation that the Appellant has been targeted by Mr. XXXX.

With respect to the RPD analysis of Exhibit P-3, the RPD questioned the Appellant on the document in a hearing setting and identified two problems with the document in addition to the fact that the Appellant returned to Puerto Nuevo on several occasions regardless of the alleged risk. I conclude that the RPD had an advantage in this analysis and did not error in its conclusion that this corroborative evidence has no probative value.

To my mind this conclusion directly feeds into the RPD's credibility concern for the inconsistency in the claim related to extortion demands. A logical problem with this whole claim is that the media and police sourced documentation portrays Mr. XXXX as a Puerto Nuevo based drug dealing thug and petty thief. The Appellant's identified risk is that Mr. XXXX is a dangerous gang member who has targeted the Appellant and his business outside Puerto Nuevo with extortion threats and has the resources to act with impunity such that he could find the Appellant wherever he might go in Peru.

As noted above, the first important inconsistency identified by the RPD relates to when Mr. XXXX allegedly began to extort money from the Appellant. The Appellant argues that the narrative is not inconsistent that it might be viewed as having some paragraphs out of order (Oral hearing at minute 2:22). The RPD cannot accept this explanation which is an interpretation which is inconsistent with a plain reading of the narrative including paragraph 12 which sets out that: "My parents and siblings were witnesses of what was going on, I kept receiving threats and money demands by the members of that gang, who were now more against me when they found out about the formal complaint filed against their leader". I conclude that the RPD did not error when it concluded that the Appellant had told his story in "chronological order" (RPD Decision, paragraph 23).

With respect to the implications of this conclusion, at best this inconsistency related to when the extortion demands began might be interpreted as embellishment. In this case the RPD concludes that the inconsistency is evidence that the extortion did not happen, on a balance of probability. This conclusion is further buttressed with the identification of an important omission in the absence of a reference in the narrative of the Appellant to his brother receiving written demands for money (RPD Decision, paragraph 25 - Oral hearing at minute 45-50). Again this is a credibility problem with the core allegation that Mr. XXXX has targeted the Appellant.

The Appellant argues that "these new three Exhibits only confirm the allegations of the claimant in the sense that he was targeted by a very dangerous man" (Appellant's Memorandum, paragraph 15). I conclude that this new evidence does not provide evidence related to whether the Appellant was targeted by Mr. XXXX. This is to say that while the RPD would accept that Mr. XXXX exists, the Appellant has not met his burden of showing that his story, that he has been targeted by Mr. XXXX and the Puerto Nuevo gang, is true, on a balance of probability because those elements of the allegations related to targeting contain inconsistencies and omission. To this must be added the RPD's analysis of the Appellant's travel both out of Peru and back and forth into the danger zone of Puerto Nuevo. I conclude that the RPD had an advantage of listening to the Appellant in a hearing setting and that this conclusion is not an error.

I would add to this analysis that in viewing the news video which is embedded in the on-line version of the news article P-5 with the provided web site citation3 it is clear that the police are willing to act against Mr. XXXX. This can also be seen in new evidence which identifies two additional arrests of Mr. XXXX and the fact that the Appellant is aware that Mr. XXXX was tried and convicted and sent to jail, albeit for a relatively short period after the 2014 arrest (Oral hearing at minute 2:36). I conclude that all this is evidence that contradicts the Appellant's allegations that Mr. XXXX can acting with impunity. Of course this assumes that Mr. XXXX is seeking to target the Appellant, which the RPD has determined has not been established. I am in agreement with this conclusion.

Overall, I conclude the RPD had an advantage in having listened to the Appellant and having reviewed the Appellant's evidence during the hearing with the Appellant present and therefore had an advantage in reaching a conclusion with respect to its credibility assessment. After reviewing all the evidence in this case, I am in agreement with this adverse assessment. I also conclude that the Appellant's appeal contains nothing in terms of argument or new evidence which is sufficient or relevant for me to reverse the RPD's first instance determination.
For all these reasons, I confirm the determination of the RPD, that Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection".

Therefore, his appeal is dismissed. Stephen J. Gallagher Stephen J. Gallagher December 8, 2015 Date /kp 1 Huruglica v. M.C.I. (2014) FC 799. 2 Njeukam v.
